## 3.1 Overview of the JuliaGeo Organization

The JuliaGeo GitHub organization was established to serve as a focal point for developing and maintaining geospatial tooling in the Julia language. It is a community of researchers, engineers, and practitioners committed to developing documented and accessible tools for spatial geometry and raster data manipulation, fostering reproducibility and interoperability in geospatial computing. The organization communicates through the Julia Discourse (julia Geo category) and the Julia Slack #geo channel.

The JuliaGeo ecosystem is organized around a layered architecture. At the foundation are low-level GDAL wrappers and geometry primitives. Above them sit higher-level data access packages that provide Tables.jl-compatible interfaces for working with vector and raster data. At the top are analysis packages including spatial statistics frameworks, accessibility calculators, and visualization tools. This architecture promotes interoperability: data loaded with one package can typically be passed directly to analysis functions from another.


## 3.2 Core Vector Data Packages


### 3.2.1 GeoInterface.jl

GeoInterface.jl defines a common protocol for geospatial vector data in Julia — a set of traits and functions that any geometry type can implement to become interoperable with the entire JuliaGeo ecosystem. It is analogous to the role played by the Python GeoJSON specification or the R sf Simple Features standard. By implementing the GeoInterface traits, a geometry type gains automatic interoperability with packages like ArchGDAL, GeoDataFrames, Turf, and GeoMakie without requiring explicit bridges.

```julia
using GeoInterface

# Check if a geometry implements GeoInterface
GeoInterface.isgeometry(geom)        # -> Bool
GeoInterface.geomtrait(geom)          # -> PolygonTrait, PointTrait, etc.
GeoInterface.coordinates(geom)        # -> Vector of coordinates
GeoInterface.ncoord(geom)             # -> number of coordinate dimensions
```


### 3.2.2 Shapefile.jl

Shapefile.jl provides native Julia support for reading and writing ESRI Shapefiles — the most ubiquitous format for geographic vector data in the public health and government data world. Census TIGER/Line files, HRSA geographic data, and most CDC GIS data are distributed as shapefiles. Shapefile.jl integrates with the Tables.jl interface, making it straightforward to load shapefile data directly into DataFrames.

```julia
using Shapefile, DataFrames

# Read a Census TIGER/Line county shapefile
table = Shapefile.Table("tl_2023_us_county.shp")
df = DataFrame(table)   # All attributes as columns

# Access geometry column
geoms = Shapefile.shapes(table)   # Vector of geometry objects

# Filter to a specific state (FIPS 38 = North Dakota)
nd_idx = findall(row -> row.STATEFP == "38", eachrow(df))
nd_geoms = geoms[nd_idx]
nd_df = df[nd_idx, :]
```


### 3.2.3 ArchGDAL.jl

ArchGDAL.jl is a comprehensive Julia wrapper for the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library (GDAL) — the de facto open-source standard for reading and writing raster and vector geospatial datasets. Through ArchGDAL, Julia can natively read over 200 vector and raster formats, including Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, GeoTIFF, NetCDF, and more. ArchGDAL provides a higher-level, more Julian API than the lower-level GDAL.jl wrapper.

```julia
using ArchGDAL

# Open a vector dataset
ArchGDAL.read("counties.shp") do dataset
    layer = ArchGDAL.getlayer(dataset, 0)
    ArchGDAL.nfeature(layer)       # Count features
    feature = ArchGDAL.nextfeature(layer)
    geom = ArchGDAL.getgeom(feature)
    ArchGDAL.geomname(geom)        # Geometry type name
    ArchGDAL.getarea(geom)         # Area in CRS units
end

# Coordinate reference system operations
src_crs = ArchGDAL.importEPSG(4326)    # WGS 84 geographic
dst_crs = ArchGDAL.importEPSG(5070)    # Conus Albers (US National)
ArchGDAL.createcoordtrans(src_crs, dst_crs) do transform
    ArchGDAL.transform!(geom, transform)
end
```


### 3.2.4 GeoDataFrames.jl

GeoDataFrames.jl provides a DataFrame-centric interface for geographic vector data, built on top of ArchGDAL. It is the Julia analogue of Python's GeoPandas. Users interact with geographic data as familiar DataFrames with a special geometry column, using standard DataFrame operations for filtering, grouping, and joining, while geographic-specific operations (spatial joins, overlay, buffer, dissolve) are provided as additional methods.

```julia
using GeoDataFrames

# Load HRSA HPSA shapefile
hpsa = GeoDataFrames.read("HPSA_Shapefiles/HPSA_Primary_Care.shp")

# Basic spatial operations
hpsa_rural = filter(row -> row.Designation_Type == "Geographic Area", hpsa)

# Spatial join: which counties intersect HPSAs?
counties = GeoDataFrames.read("tl_2023_us_county.shp")
county_hpsa = GeoDataFrames.innerjoin(counties, hpsa_rural;
    on = :geometry => :geometry, kind = :intersects)

# Calculate area of each HPSA polygon
hpsa.area_km2 = GeoDataFrames.area(hpsa) ./ 1e6  # m² to km²

# Write result
GeoDataFrames.write("rural_hpsa_counties.shp", county_hpsa)
```


## 3.3 Core Raster Data Packages


### 3.3.1 Rasters.jl

Rasters.jl is the central raster data package in the Julia ecosystem. It provides a unified type system for working with gridded spatial data — satellite imagery, digital elevation models, environmental exposure grids, and continuous surface estimates. Rasters.jl integrates with DimensionalData.jl for dimension-aware indexing, supports lazy reading of large files via memory mapping, and provides high-performance raster algebra operations that take full advantage of Julia's broadcasting system.

```julia
using Rasters, RasterDataSources

# Download and load population density raster (LandScan or WorldPop)
# (RasterDataSources.jl handles downloads from standard repositories)

# Load a local GeoTIFF (e.g., CDC county-level mortality raster)
mortality_raster = Raster("county_mortality.tif")

# Inspect
size(mortality_raster)        # Grid dimensions
dims(mortality_raster)        # X/Y/time dimensions
crs(mortality_raster)         # Coordinate reference system

# Crop to a bounding box (e.g., North Dakota)
bbox = Rasters.Extents.Extent(X = (-104.0, -96.5), Y = (45.9, 49.0))
nd_mortality = crop(mortality_raster; to = bbox)

# Reproject to Albers Equal Area
nd_albers = resample(nd_mortality; crs = EPSG(5070))

# Raster algebra: normalize to rates per 100,000
population = Raster("population.tif")
rate_raster = (mortality_raster ./ population) .* 100_000
```


## 3.4 Spatial Statistics and Geostatistics


### 3.4.1 GeoStats.jl

GeoStats.jl is an extensible framework for high-performance geostatistics in Julia, maintained by Júlio Hoffimann. It provides a unified interface to a comprehensive suite of geostatistical methods including variogram estimation, kriging (ordinary, simple, universal, indicator), simulation methods, and spatial cross-validation. GeoStats.jl is particularly valuable for population health applications that involve estimating continuous surfaces from point-sampled data — for example, estimating provider density surfaces or environmental exposure concentrations from sparse sampling points.

```julia
using GeoStats, GeoTables

# Create a GeoTable from county health data
# GeoStats expects data wrapped in a GeoTable with associated geometries
health_data = GeoTable(df; geometry = :geom_col)

# Compute empirical variogram for cardiovascular mortality
γ = EmpiricalVariogram(health_data, :cvd_mortality; nlags = 30)

# Fit a theoretical variogram model
fitted = fit(SphericalVariogram, γ)

# Ordinary kriging interpolation to a fine grid
problem = EstimationProblem(health_data, target_grid, :cvd_mortality)
solver = Kriging(:cvd_mortality => (variogram = fitted,))
solution = solve(problem, solver)

# Cross-validation
cv = LeaveOneOut()
errors = validate(problem, solver, cv)
```


### 3.4.2 Turf.jl

Turf.jl is a spatial analysis library written in Julia, ported from the widely-used Turf.js JavaScript library. It provides a comprehensive set of geometric operations and spatial analysis functions including distance calculations, point-in-polygon testing, spatial clustering, polygon buffering, intersection, union, and various geometric transformations. For healthcare accessibility analysis, Turf.jl provides the building blocks for implementing floating catchment area methods and network-free accessibility measures.

```julia
using Turf

# Point and feature creation
patient = Turf.point([-97.5, 46.8])    # lon, lat for Bismarck ND area
hospital = Turf.point([-100.7, 46.9])

# Distance in kilometers
d_km = Turf.distance(patient, hospital; units = "kilometers")

# Buffer: create 30km catchment area around hospital
catchment = Turf.buffer(hospital, 30; units = "kilometers")

# Check if patient is within catchment
within = Turf.boolean_point_in_polygon(patient, catchment)

# Centroid of a county polygon
centroid = Turf.centroid(county_polygon)
```


## 3.5 Visualization and Mapping


### 3.5.1 GeoMakie.jl

GeoMakie.jl is the primary cartographic visualization package in the Julia ecosystem. Built on top of the Makie.jl high-performance graphics system, GeoMakie adds geographic projections, coastlines, administrative boundaries, and spatial data rendering capabilities. It supports interactive plots (via GLMakie or WGLMakie backends) and publication-quality static maps (via CairoMakie). For healthcare GIS work, GeoMakie enables the creation of choropleth maps, dot density maps, accessibility surface maps, and multi-panel comparative geographic displays.

```julia
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie

fig = Figure(resolution = (1200, 800))
ga = GeoAxis(fig[1,1];
    dest = "+proj=laea +lat_0=45 +lon_0=-100 +ellps=WGS84",  # Albers-like
    title = "Primary Care Health Professional Shortage Areas")

# Draw US state boundaries
lines!(ga, GeoMakie.coastlines())
poly!(ga, states_geoms; color = :white, strokecolor = :gray, strokewidth = 0.5)

# Choropleth: shade counties by HPSA score
poly!(ga, county_geoms;
    color = hpsa_scores,
    colormap = :Reds,
    colorrange = (0, 25),
    strokecolor = :white,
    strokewidth = 0.2)

Colorbar(fig[1,2]; colormap = :Reds, limits = (0,25),
    label = "HPSA Designation Score")

save("hpsa_map.pdf", fig)
```
